t: 8 Things Teachers Do To Cause Boredom
q: For where there is boredom, there is misbehavior percolating just under the surface, ready to pounce.

Many teachers misunderstand the oft-heard mandate for more rigor. They take it to mean that they need to make their instruction more complex, more involved, more verbose—which is a major reason why students don’t progress.

Most standard grade-level subject matter is interesting, but your students don’t know that. In fact, many assume, based on their learning experiences in the past, that it’s boring. It’s your job to show them otherwise.

Teachers who struggle with classroom management tend to talk endlessly about behavior. They hold class meetings. They hash things out. They revisit the same tired topic over and over, much to their students’ eye-rolling chagrin.

And when students cross that line and into boredom, misbehavior is sure to follow. The good news is that by avoiding the common mistakes listed above, you can keep boredom at bay and inspired learning in the spotlight.

Eight specific teacher habits — including sitting too long, over-talking, and over-complicating content — are identified as direct causes of student boredom.

Talking about behavior in class meetings and discussions, rather than taking direct action, is listed among the causes of disengagement.
He closes by framing boredom as a fine line just past productive time-on-task, arguing that avoiding these eight mistakes keeps students both engaged and well-behaved.

t: How To Talk To Difficult Students
q: Most teachers talk to difficult students too much, because somewhere along the line they’ve gotten the idea that the more attention they give them, the better teacher they’ll be.
In a desperate attempt to improve behavior, many teachers will say just about anything to difficult students—regardless of its truthfulness.

Never ask them why they did this or that. Never force assurances or explanations. Never give them a dressing-down. Let their mistakes and subsequent accountability, or their successes and subsequent good feelings, be the lesson.
By simply not making a big deal out of them doing what they’re supposed to do, what they’re expected to do, you send a powerful, behavior-altering message.
But the more attention you give to difficult students, the less attention they’ll pay to what you say and the harder it will be to improve their behavior.
x: Linsin argues that most teachers talk to difficult students far too much, mistakenly believing that extra attention itself improves behavior.

Sometimes the most powerful response to good behavior from a difficult student is saying nothing at all, avoiding the appearance of a 'parade' for expected behavior.

t: 2 Easy Ways To Build Rapport With Your Students
q: Rapport is nothing more than a connection you make with your students based on their positive feelings for you.

To build genuine rapport, you have to draw students to you. You have to use your personality, your humor, and your charisma to get students to want to be around you and take an interest in who you are.
What it does is allow you to make an instant positive and personal connection with each student. It communicates a thousand wonderful things in just a couple of seconds.
Telling a story about your childhood is a good place to start. It places you in an environment they’re unfamiliar picturing you in, but one in which they can closely identify with.

Many teachers have a hard time building rapport because they respond emotionally to misbehavior. They show frustration, they scold, they lecture, and in so doing they erect a giant wall between themselves and their students.
x: Linsin defines rapport as a connection rooted in students' positive feelings for a teacher, and clarifies that it can't be forced through direct, awkward questioning.
Building rapport is framed as partly about restraint — avoiding emotional reactions to misbehavior that erect walls between teacher and student.
The 'smile until they smile' technique — used during attendance or passing back work — creates instant, low-effort personal connection with each student.
Telling a personal childhood story is presented as a uniquely powerful rapport-building tool, provided it involves adventure or comedic mishap rather than something overly sensitive.

t: 5 Strategies To Avoid With Difficult Students oid-with-difficult-students/
q: Any strategy that involves a “do this and get that” scenario weakens over time and does nothing to spark intrinsic motivation—which is the one ingredient necessary for real, lasting improvement.
Most of the time the student being ignored will respond by ratcheting up his or her attention-getting behavior, at times going so far as to sing, yell, or even laugh while you’re trying to teach.

Recess time-out only works if you, as the classroom teacher, are the one doing the supervising. Otherwise, it’s a weak consequence, sitting there with a whole band of troublemakers from all over the school.
Permanent time-out merely reinforces in the student’s mind that he or she is a behavior problem. It becomes part of who they are, like their eye color or where they were born.
Most difficult students are able to make lasting changes in behavior when they’re subject to the same solid classroom management plan as everybody else.
x: Behavior contracts produce fast but short-lived improvement while labeling students and undermining intrinsic motivation over time.
